strengths: Compelling training-free paradigm: Unlike the majority of recent video reasoning segmentation methods that require LoRA or full-decoder fine-tuning, DecAF achieves strong performance purely at inference time by exploiting intrinsic MLLM attention maps.

Well-motivated technical design: The paper addresses known pitfalls of transformer attention (attention sinks, noise, temporal vs. spatial resolution trade-offs) through well-engineered components—specifically contrastive object-background fusion, multi-scale complementary video-frame fusion, and an attention consistency score for SAM2 candidate pruning.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: The authors evaluate on five diverse benchmarks (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, ReVOS) across three modern MLLM architectures (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5-VL) and various parameter scales (2B to 14B).

Competitive performance: DecAF substantially outperforms existing training-free approaches (Loc-Head, TAM) by large margins and matches or even surpasses several specialized training-based models (e.g., VISA, VideoLISA, GLUS).

Comprehensive ablation studies: Every component of the framework is systematically ablated, including the contrastive mechanism, frame-video complementing, multi-scale inputs, rollout normalization, layer selection, and tracklet scoring formulations.
weaknesses: Computational overhead and inference latency: The method requires multiple MLLM forward passes (video object prompt, video background prompt, per-frame object/background passes, and category selection) along with attention rollout tracking and SAM2 propagation. The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of inference time, memory footprint, and latency compared to single-pass or training-based baselines.

Error propagation in the prompting pipeline: Contrastive fusion relies on successfully extracting the correct object category from an initial prompt. If the category is incorrectly identified, the background-exclusion prompt will be flawed, potentially suppressing the true target object.

Heavy reliance on SAM2 for boundary delineation: As shown in Table 1, the raw attention masks alone achieve modest performance (~20-25 J&F), indicating that SAM2 does the critical heavy lifting for fine-grained contours. While standard in training-free grounding, the method fundamentally acts as a point-prompt generator for SAM2 rather than an end-to-end segmentation model.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: training-free video reasoning segmentation, which bypasses the heavy computational and annotation costs associated with fine-tuning MLLMs and video mask decoders.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across five widely used datasets (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, and ReVOS) and three major MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5-VL) across multiple model sizes.

Strong experimental results: DecAF significantly outperforms prior training-free baselines (Loc-Head and TAM) both with raw attention masks and with SAM2 prompting, achieving competitive results even against specialized training-based models.

Extensive ablation studies and analyses that validate individual design components, including object-background contrastive fusion, video-frame complementary fusion, vision-aware rollout normalization, and attention consistency tracklet scoring.
weaknesses: High inference latency and computational complexity: The approach requires multiple forward passes of the MLLM (object-level query, frame-level passes, and contrastive background query), full-layer attention rollout caching/multiplication, and multi-candidate SAM2 tracklet propagation. An empirical runtime, memory, and latency analysis is missing.

Heavy reliance on intermediate text categorization: The contrastive background prompt depends on correctly predicting the target object category via prompting. For ambiguous, abstract, or multi-faceted queries where categorical identification fails, the error can cascade into corrupted background attention subtraction.

Heuristic nature of the pipeline: The framework relies on several engineered thresholds and filtering criteria (e.g., τ_pq, τ_trk, IoU NMS threshold, layer cutoff, δ penalty). While empirical ablations show reasonable stability, the framework combines several hand-crafted heuristics rather than a unified formulation.

strengths: Compelling and timely problem formulation: Investigating the intrinsic spatio-temporal localization capability of MLLMs without task-specific fine-tuning or mask decoder training is highly valuable and practically relevant.

Well-motivated technical design: DecAF addresses fundamental issues of attention rollout in MLLMs (attention sinks and visual noise) through an intuitive contrastive object-background fusion and multi-scale video-frame complementary fusion.

Effective integration with SAM2: The attention-guided prompting and attention consistency score ($s^{ac}$) provide a principled mechanism to suppress false-positive tracklets and significantly enhance mask quality without relying on heuristic bounding box extraction.

Extensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is validated across five benchmarks (Ref-DAVIS, ReasonVOS, ReVOS, MeViS, Ref-YTVOS) and four MLLM architectures (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL), substantially outperforming prior training-free baselines and achieving performance competitive with fully fine-tuned models.

Thorough ablations and error analysis: The paper provides granular ablations for each algorithmic component (contrastive fusion, multi-scale fusion, attention rollout layer, tracklet scoring) as well as honest discussions of failure cases.
weaknesses: Inference latency and computational overhead: DecAF requires multiple MLLM forward passes per video sample (both video-level and frame-by-frame forward passes for object and background prompts, plus category selection). The paper lacks runtime, memory consumption, or throughput analysis comparing DecAF against single-pass training-based methods.

Sensitivity to object category extraction: The background prompt relies on accurately extracting the target object class name from the expression. If the model fails or hallucinates an incorrect class during this initial step, the subsequent contrastive attention map could degrade or suppress the true target.

Minor terminology inconsistencies: The method is referred to as 'Decomposed Attention Fusion' in the title and abstract, but occasionally termed 'Decoupled Attention Fusion' in Section 3.1 and Section 4.3.

strengths: Compelling and practical training-free paradigm: The paper tackles video reasoning segmentation without expensive joint training or fine-tuning of MLLMs and segmentation foundation models, demonstrating strong zero-shot localization capabilities inherent to MLLMs.

Technically sound and well-motivated design: The proposed Decomposed Attention Fusion (DecAF) effectively addresses key failure modes in transformer attention maps—namely, visual attention sinks and coarse video token resolution—via contrastive object-background subtraction and complementary video-frame fusion.

Effective integration with SAM2: The attention-guided prompting strategy, coupled with the attention consistency score ($s^{ac}$), effectively filters out spurious tracklets and resolves the mismatch between low-resolution attention maps and high-fidelity video segmentation masks.

Extensive and convincing empirical validation: The framework is benchmarked across five diverse datasets (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, and ReVOS) and four MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL, Qwen2.5VL) across multiple scales. It substantially outperforms prior training-free methods (e.g., Loc-Head, TAM) and is competitive with or superior to several specialized training-based approaches on reasoning-intensive benchmarks.

Thorough ablations and robustness analyses: The authors provide detailed ablation studies on each component (V-Max normalization, fusion types, starting layers, scoring metrics, prompt variants in Appendix F, and native grounding baselines in Appendix E).
weaknesses: Inference latency and computational cost: DecAF requires multiple forward passes per sample (video-level passes for object and background, plus individual frame-level passes for complementary fusion). The paper lacks an explicit quantification of inference run-time, memory footprint, or FPS comparison against baselines like Loc-Head or standard MLLM inference.

Dependence on accurate category extraction for background prompting: The background contrastive prompt relies on intermediate text generation of the object class label ({Object category}). While prompt robustness is evaluated, potential failure propagation when the MLLM misclassifies or encounters abstract/ambiguous non-explicit referents warrants deeper quantitative analysis.

Contour accuracy remains heavily reliant on SAM2: As shown in Table 1, the raw attention masks alone achieve modest performance ($J\&F \approx 20\text{--}25$), indicating that while MLLM attention provides coarse spatial pointing, SAM2 is doing the heavy lifting for precise object boundary delineation.

strengths: Well-motivated training-free framework: The paper tackles a challenging problem—video reasoning segmentation without task-specific training—by effectively unlocking and probing the inherent grounding signals within generalist MLLMs.

Effective technical design (DecAF): The proposed decomposed attention fusion cleverly addresses core limitations of raw attention rollout: (1) contrastive object-background subtraction effectively mitigates visual attention sinks, and (2) video-frame complementary fusion balances long-range temporal context with high-resolution frame-level spatial cues.

Well-designed SAM2 prompting and filtering pipeline: The attention consistency score ($s^{ac}$) offers a principled, training-free mechanism to filter out spurious mask tracklets caused by low-granularity attention activations before propagating via SAM2.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation: The method is validated across five benchmarks (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, and ReVOS) and three modern MLLM architectures (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5-VL). DecAF substantially outperforms existing training-free baselines (Loc-Head, TAM) and achieves performance competitive with fully fine-tuned methods.

Thorough ablations and supplementary analysis: The authors provide detailed ablation studies isolating each component (contrastive fusion, multi-scale frame/video fusion, rollout normalization, layers, thresholds), alongside extensive prompt sensitivity analysis and failure case discussions.
weaknesses: Inference latency and computational overhead: The framework requires multiple forward passes through the MLLM (object query, background query, video-level and per-frame evaluations) followed by SAM2 mask propagation and scoring. A quantitative analysis of inference time, FLOPs, and GPU memory usage compared to single-pass or training-based methods is not provided.

Dependence on explicit intermediate object naming: The contrastive background prompt relies on extracting an explicit target object category name ($O_{name}$). When expressions involve abstract references, ambiguous categories, or multiple interacting entities of the same class, inaccurate category extraction could degrade the quality of the negative attention map.

Significant reliance on SAM2 for mask boundary quality: As evidenced by Table 1 vs. Table 2, raw attention maps achieve relatively low mask fidelity ($J\&F \approx 20\text{--}25$), indicating that MLLM attention functions primarily as a coarse point/region generator while SAM2 carries the heavy lifting for boundary delineation.

Minor terminology inconsistencies and typos: The method is introduced as 'Decomposed Attention Fusion' in the title and abstract, but referred to as 'Decoupled Attention Fusion' in Section 3.1 and Section 4.3. Additionally, Table 9 contains typos such as 'Fisrt frame'.

strengths: Compelling Training-Free Formulation: Proposing a fully training-free framework for video reasoning segmentation is timely and practically valuable, avoiding the substantial compute and data requirements of jointly fine-tuning MLLMs and SAM.

Well-Motivated Attention Fusion Strategies: The combination of contrastive object-background fusion (which effectively counters the visual attention sink phenomenon without model-specific heuristics) and complementary video-frame fusion (balancing temporal context with high-resolution spatial fidelity) is intuitive and technically sound.

Strong and Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation: The paper evaluates across five established referring and reasoning VOS benchmarks (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, ReVOS) and three major MLLM architectures (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5-VL). DecAF substantially outperforms existing training-free baselines (Loc-Head, TAM) and matches or exceeds several supervised/fine-tuned approaches.

Rigorous Ablations and Thorough Analysis: The paper provides extensive ablations analyzing each component (contrastive fusion, multi-scale framing, head-weighted rollout normalization, starting layer depth, SAM prompting thresholds, tracklet scoring, and prompt sensitivity).
weaknesses: High Computational and Inference Overhead: DecAF requires multiple MLLM forward passes per video sample (object-focused video QA, background video QA, and corresponding frame-level passes, plus category choice prompt) alongside attention rollout matrix computation across layers. A quantitative breakdown of runtime, latency per video, and GPU peak memory footprint compared to single-pass and training-based methods is missing.

Pipeline Complexity and Heuristic Dependencies: The framework involves multiple sequential stages and hand-tuned hyperparameters/heuristics (e.g., choice of starting layer, threshold tau_pq, tau_trk, NMS threshold of 0.7, mean thresholding with penalty delta_t). The performance depends on carefully balancing these thresholds.

Vulnerability to Early Object Classification Errors: Contrastive background suppression relies on correctly identifying the object category string via prompting. If the MLLM misclassifies or generates an incorrect category label for complex/abstract expressions, the background-focused prompt could erroneously suppress foreground details or fail to eliminate background distractors.

Heavy Reliance on SAM2 for Accurate Boundaries: As shown in Table 1, the attention maps alone provide very low contour accuracy (F scores around 10-18% and J&F around 15-25%), indicating that the attention maps act strictly as rough coarse point seeds, while the precise segmentation capability is largely outsourced to SAM2.
